title: Holding Government to Account on Nature, Water and Waste
label: 9 September 2026 · OEP evidence session
summary: Members of the Lords Environment and Climate Change Committee questioned the Office for Environmental Protection (OEP) about its priorities, powers and effectiveness. Dame Helen Ghosh (chair) and Natalie Prosser (CEO) explained the OEP’s limited budget, its top priorities (nature-friendly farming, water reform and marine issues), how it works with other regulators, and how it uses investigations and, rarely, legal action to change public-authority behaviour. The session also covered worrying findings on regulated waste inspections, the slow progress on statutory nature targets, and concerns about planning, water use (including data centres) and biodiversity net gain.

chapters.title: Who the OEP is and its immediate priorities
chapters.takeaway: The OEP, newly chaired by Dame Helen, must prioritise with reduced real-terms funding and will focus on nature-friendly farming, water reform and marine health.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. Could you introduce yourselves for the record?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: I became OEP chair on 1 June. Before this I worked in the Civil Service, Defra and the National Trust, so I know environmental issues and public bodies.

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: I'm the OEP chief executive and have led the organisation for about five years.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Helen, what are your plans as new chair?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We have a funding problem: flat cash for England and Northern Ireland means a real-terms cut. So we must prioritise what will make the biggest difference.

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: Top priorities are nature-friendly farming, water reform (post-Cunliffe review), marine issues and in Northern Ireland managing nutrients from farms and sewage.

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We’re updating our three-year strategy and welcome input from the committee as we choose what to keep and what to focus on.

chapters.title: The OEP’s role, powers and when it uses legal action
chapters.takeaway: The OEP mostly uses transparency, reports and targeted investigations to change practice, but can issue binding decision notices and, rarely, take formal legal action if needed.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: You don’t enforce everything—how do you split up work with other regulators, and how will you prioritise enforcement?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We’re not the regulator of regulators. We scrutinise public authorities like the Environment Agency, Ofwat and Natural England, work closely with them, and use tools like information notices and investigations.

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We usually change practice by making failures public and proposing practical fixes. Our most serious step is a decision notice; the last resort is an environmental review (like a judicial review).

turns.speaker: Lord Jay of Ewelme
turns.text: Might you use judicial review more to send a stronger signal?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: Possibly. We’d use environmental review if there’s grave disagreement about what the law means or where outcomes are so poor that only a court can clarify obligations.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: If government policy doesn’t change and we miss 2030 targets, what more can the OEP do?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We push for clear delivery plans, milestones and measurable indicators. Our reports aim to make failures transparent and to get Ministers to act—statutory targets are the Government’s responsibility.

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: We provide objective evidence on progress. If Ministers aren’t meeting legal targets, that’s ultimately for them to fix—our role is monitoring, reporting and, where necessary, acting.

chapters.title: Water, farming and planning concerns
chapters.takeaway: The OEP is investigating water law compliance, worries about overreliance on small farming schemes, and flags planning gaps like drainage rules and biodiversity net gain changes.

turns.speaker: Baroness McIntosh of Pickering
turns.text: Are you assessing whether the Government is on track with statutory nature targets, and what about water law after EU rules?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: EIP23 showed the Government off track on many targets. We're publishing a progress report in January; we don’t expect major improvement yet. We’re investigating water framework directive (WFD) compliance now.

turns.speaker: Baroness McIntosh of Pickering
turns.text: What about surface water drainage standards (SUDS) and planning conflicts—are you worried?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: Yes. If SUDS aren’t mandatory and water companies aren’t statutory consultees, sewage risks rise. That’s a planning and Defra issue we’re watching.

turns.speaker: Lord Trees
turns.text: On biodiversity net gain (BNG), are brownfield sites being exempted? And should big water users like data centres be consulted on water planning?

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: BNG is under threat from exclusions and restrictions on local standards; it hasn’t settled in yet and we’re concerned. On data centres, they add real pressure in thirsty regions—water reform needs to tackle scarcity and demand from business.

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We’re worried about loss of BNG protections. No final decision on brownfield exemptions yet. For water, Defra’s Secretary of State is conscious of resilience, but reforms must handle scarcity as well as pollution.

turns.speaker: Baroness Coffey
turns.text: Do the new environmental delivery plans (EDPs) strengthen the chance of meeting the apex statutory target to halt species decline?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: EDPs could help because they aim for clearer delivery and measurement, but it depends on Natural England having the resources to implement and monitor them.

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: It’s early to tell. The first EDP is a narrow pilot on nutrients; whether EDPs overall help the 2030 target is still uncertain.

chapters.title: Waste inspections and the leakages undermining a circular economy
chapters.takeaway: The OEP found major problems in the Environment Agency’s inspections of permitted waste sites; these gaps feed illegal tipping and threaten efforts to move to a circular economy.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: Your waste inspections report said the Environment Agency’s regulated-site checks are poor. How did they respond?

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: We’d engaged with the Agency beforehand. The report was hard-hitting and showed weak inspection quality. The Agency has engaged and accepted recommendations; their formal response is imminent.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: Have you had whistleblowers from the EA?

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: Yes, we’ve had whistleblowers from public authorities we oversee; I won’t give details but we did receive several in the last reporting period.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Our committee found 38 million tonnes of illegally managed waste a year—mainly from permitted sites. That’s huge. Are the EA’s false positives undermining the circular economy?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: Yes. We’ll say in our EIP25 report that the targets to reduce illegal waste aren’t strong enough. That level of leakage is shocking and must be addressed.

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: A proper waste resources strategy is essential. The regulated and illegal problems are linked to how we use materials and the incentives in the system.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: Are there lessons from waste inspection failures that apply across government enforcement?

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: Yes. We see inconsistent inspection regimes and a tendency to be resource-driven. We need coherent, risk-based regulation, consistent data and better targeting of the biggest harms.

chapters.title: How the OEP holds government to account and next steps
chapters.takeaway: The OEP will keep using reports, investigations, monitoring and, where needed, legal tools to press ministers and regulators to deliver statutory targets, but it needs clearer delivery plans and proper funding across government.

turns.speaker: Lord Redwood
turns.text: Can you give a concrete example where the OEP changed practice and the benefit was clear?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: Our combined-sewage-outflows investigation clarified how laws apply and changed operational practice by Defra, the Environment Agency and Ofwat. Clarifying law can alter behaviour quickly.

turns.speaker: Lord Jay of Ewelme
turns.text: Will you increase enforcement if problems persist?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We’ll use the full toolkit. We’ve achieved change by transparency and negotiated fixes so far, but we won’t rule out stronger legal steps if necessary.

turns.speaker: Baroness Coffey
turns.text: Do you follow up to ensure court rulings and commitments are actually implemented?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: Yes. The board has agreed we must shine a light on compliance after reports and ensure undertakings lead to real outcomes; that follow-up will be part of our strategy.

turns.speaker: Lord Trees
turns.text: You said nature-friendly farming matters—have you influenced the sustainable farming incentive (SFI)?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We’ve urged that SFI alone won’t be enough; higher-tier schemes that deliver real habitat recovery need proper funding. We’re running an inquiry to advise on the whole system.

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: Defra has taken our recommendations seriously and shown more transparency on SFI rollout. But the key is delivery and investability across the whole land-use system.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are Ministers hearing you that statutory targets aren’t being met?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We make our findings public and send them to Parliament. Statutory targets sit with Ministers; we provide evidence and press for clear, funded delivery plans.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both for your time. Any final words?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We’re committed to using our powers to get better environmental outcomes despite limited resources. We’ll focus on what makes the biggest difference.

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: We’ll keep monitoring, reporting and engaging with regulators and Ministers so the law means real improvement on the ground.
